summary: Small, easy-to-catch flatfish taken from wharves, shallow bays, and estuary mouths on mud-sand bottom, best in spring and early summer on light bottom tackle with worms or clams.

sections.heading: Know the Fish
sections.body_md:
Winter flounder (*Pseudopleuronectes americanus*, also called blackback or mud dab locally) are a right-eyed flatfish — both eyes sit on the right side of the body, with the eyed side showing a brown, reddish-brown, olive-green, or almost-black coloring that shifts to match the bottom, and the blind (underside) side pale white. The lateral line is nearly straight (not strongly arched like some other flatfish), the tail is rounded, and the mouth is small with few or no teeth — a key reason small hooks out-produce big ones.

Most fish caught from shore run well under the maximum size — DFO lists winter flounder growing to roughly 50 cm (about 20 in), with males living around 11 years and females around 12, though some sources report fish to 15+ years and 58 cm in slower-growing populations. They're sight feeders, most active by day, and prefer a narrow water temperature band of about 12–15°C, which drives predictable seasonal movement: into shallow bays and inshore flats when the water is in that range, off into deeper/cooler water when it isn't.

sections.heading: When to Go
sections.body_md:
### Season
Spring through early summer is the classic shore window in this region — fish move into shallow inshore flats, estuary mouths, and harbours to feed and spawn as water temperatures come into their preferred 12–15°C range, then drift back to deeper, cooler water as summer peaks. Local anglers report the best shore fishing from roughly April/May into July, tapering as water warms.

### Spawning
DFO's species profile notes winter flounder in the Bay of Fundy region spawn inshore in spring (May), conducted mostly at night; more broadly across their range spawning runs late winter into early spring (the fish's namesake season), with regional timing varying by latitude and water temperature. No direct spawning-timing study exists specifically for the southern Gulf of St. Lawrence stock.

### Tide
Local reports consistently favor high tide through the start of the falling tide — fish move onto shallow flats and into creek/harbour mouths to feed as the tide floods, then start dropping back as it ebbs. PEI tourism guidance specifically calls out high-to-falling tide as the productive window.

sections.heading: Where to Find Them
sections.body_md:
Winter flounder sit on soft mud, sand, or pebbled bottom in fairly shallow water (DFO notes usually under 100 m, but shore anglers are typically working single-digit-to-low-teens feet of depth) — river mouths, harbour flats, and the edges of channels and sandbars are the pattern to look for everywhere in this region.

**New Brunswick (Bay of Fundy side):** Beaver Harbour wharf is a locally reported producer for flounder (along with mackerel and bluefish); Dipper Harbour wharf is fished for flounder as the tide comes in. Forum consensus is that Bay of Fundy flounder hold in about 10 ft of water and move in and out with the tide to stay near that depth.

**Nova Scotia:** Eastern Passage, particularly around the sandbar off McCormacks Beach near the boardwalk, and the channel down toward Fisherman's Cove, are reported producers in the Halifax Harbour area. More generally, river mouths and tidal channels along the Nova Scotia coast hold fish.

**Prince Edward Island:** The Old Rustico breakwater wharf, Northport Harbour near Alberton (fishable directly off the wharf), and the MacIntyre Creek bridge on Route 350 in Canavoy are all named local spots. Charlottetown Harbour is another commonly fished area for shore anglers.

These are angler-reported locations from local forums and tourism sources, not DFO-designated fishing grounds — access, bottom conditions, and productivity change season to season, so treat them as starting points.

sections.heading: Gear
sections.body_md:
| Item | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Rod | Light spinning rod, 6–7 ft — this is a light-tackle, finesse fishery; a heavy rod masks the soft bite. |
| Reel | Small-to-medium spinning reel with 8–10 lb mono or light braid. |
| Rig | Hi-lo (two-hook) bottom rig with a pyramid or bank sinker just heavy enough to hold bottom in the current — the standard PEI/Maritime setup for shore flounder. |
| Hooks | Small — size 6–10 long-shank or wide-gap — matched to the flounder's small mouth. |
| Bait | Sandworms/bloodworms or clam strips are the standard local bait; cut fish, squid, mackerel, herring, and shrimp are also reported to work when worms aren't available. |
| Extras | Small cooler with ice, a rag for handling slimy fish, needle-nose pliers for small hooks set deep in a small mouth. |

sections.heading: Technique
sections.body_md:
Winter flounder fishing is a slow, patient, stationary game — not a search-and-cover-water fishery like mackerel or striped bass.

1. Find a flat, channel edge, or sandbar near a harbour mouth, wharf, or river mouth with mud/sand bottom and a couple feet to low double-digit feet of water on the tide you're fishing.
2. Bait both hooks of the hi-lo rig with a piece of sandworm/bloodworm or a clam strip — small pieces; flounder have small mouths and pick at bait rather than inhaling it.
3. Cast out and let the rig settle to bottom. Keep the rod tip low and watch it, or hold the line lightly between two fingers — flounder bite as light taps and nibbles, not hard strikes.
4. Resist striking on the first tap. Let the fish mouth the bait for a few seconds — flounder often peck at bait repeatedly before committing — then come tight with a firm, steady sweep rather than a hard snap.
5. If nothing happens after 10–15 minutes in one spot, especially near slack tide, move a short distance along the flat/channel edge rather than waiting it out — flounder aren't evenly distributed even within a good area.
6. Fish the high-to-falling tide window where possible; activity drops off noticeably as the flat empties out on a big ebb.

sections.heading: Handling & Release
sections.body_md:
Winter flounder have a small mouth, so hooks can go in deep on a missed hookset — use needle-nose pliers rather than fingers, and keep a hook-out tool handy for fish that are gut- or gill-hooked.

- If you're keeping fish to eat, bleed and ice them promptly like any other bottom fish — flatfish flesh holds up well but still benefits from quick icing on a warm day.
- Given the documented long-term decline of this stock in the southern Gulf of St. Lawrence (see Conservation notes below), consider releasing fish you don't intend to eat, and handle release fish quickly and with wet hands to protect the slime coat.
- No Canadian federal mercury consumption advisory specific to winter flounder turned up in this research — flatfish generally test low for mercury compared to large predatory species, but no NB/NS/PEI-specific advisory was found to cite directly.

sections.heading: Conservation & Regulatory Notes
sections.body_md:
This is the section anglers in this region most need to read before keeping fish.

**Stock decline (southern Gulf of St. Lawrence, NAFO Division 4T):** The commercial winter flounder Total Allowable Catch was cut from 1,000 tonnes to 300 tonnes in 2012 as the stock declined, then cut again to 150 tonnes in 2022 with no sign of rebuilding. In February 2023, DFO fully closed the directed commercial winter flounder fishery in 4T (winter flounder is now bycatch-only in other groundfish fisheries, at a 150-tonne annual allocation with per-trip bycatch caps being tightened through 2027). A formal rebuilding plan for the stock was approved in March 2024. Winter flounder size-at-maturity has also dropped over time — from roughly 22–24 cm in the 1970s to about 17 cm now — a sign of sustained fishing/environmental pressure on the stock.

**Recreational fishing is NOT closed.** DFO's own rebuilding-plan documentation confirms an authorized recreational groundfish fishery with access to winter flounder remains open in Maritime Provinces waters, and states no removal estimates exist for recreational catch — DFO's qualitative read is that recreational take is likely minimal since most anglers in the aggregate groundfish fishery are targeting cod. Given the commercial closure and confirmed stock decline, fish conservatively and lean toward releasing surplus catch.

**How the recreational bag limit works — this is not a flounder-specific limit.** In both DFO regions covering NB/NS/PEI, winter flounder falls under the general recreational "groundfish" aggregate bag limit alongside cod, haddock, pollock, and other groundfish — there is no flounder-specific bag or size limit in either region's notices. See the regulations table below for the current numbers by province, and note the Gulf Region limit differs from the Maritimes Region limit (Atlantic-coast NS and Bay of Fundy).

variants.name: Atlantic Halibut
variants.how_to_tell: Both are right-eyed flatfish, so eye side alone will NOT tell them apart — this is the important trap. The reliable checks are the lateral line and mouth: halibut has a lateral line that arcs sharply above the pectoral fin (winter flounder's lateral line runs nearly straight), and a large, gaping mouth that extends back to the eyes (winter flounder's mouth is small, built for picking at worms and clams). Halibut also has a concave/forked tail versus winter flounder's rounded tail, and even a small halibut is proportionally more elongated and diamond-shaped than a winter flounder of the same length.
variants.where_found: Halibut are typically a deeper, offshore fish, but juveniles can turn up inshore in the same soft-bottom flats and channels winter flounder are caught from — the overlap is real, not theoretical.
variants.notes: Atlantic halibut is ZERO RETENTION year-round in these waters under both DFO Gulf and Maritimes Region rules, with no exceptions in the aggregate groundfish bag limits. Keeping even a small halibut mistaken for a large winter flounder is a genuine regulatory violation, not a technicality — check the lateral-line arc and mouth size on anything unusually large or big-mouthed before it goes in the cooler, and release any halibut immediately.

variants.name: Yellowtail Flounder
variants.how_to_tell: Yellowtail flounder has a yellow tail fin and yellow-edged dorsal/anal fins, a thinner body, and large rusty-red irregular spots on an olive-brown back — all absent on winter flounder, which runs plain brown to almost black with no yellow trim. Yellowtail also has an arched lateral line versus winter flounder's nearly straight one, though both share a small mouth.
variants.where_found: More of an offshore/deeper-water species than winter flounder, less commonly encountered from shore in this region.
variants.notes: Both count toward the same groundfish aggregate bag limit, so misidentifying one for the other has no regulatory consequence here, but the yellow tail is a fast, reliable field check if it comes up.

variants.name: American Plaice
variants.how_to_tell: American plaice has a distinctly larger mouth than winter flounder's small worm-picking mouth, a rounded tail, and a nearly straight lateral line, with a reddish-brown eyed side. The larger mouth is the fastest check against winter flounder specifically.
variants.where_found: Deeper offshore bottom generally, less of a shore-caught fish than winter flounder in this region.
variants.notes: Counts toward the same groundfish aggregate bag limit as winter flounder — no separate rule to worry about, just worth knowing if a bigger-mouthed flatfish turns up on flounder gear.

variants.name: Witch Flounder
variants.how_to_tell: Witch flounder is narrower and less oval than winter flounder, with a small head and mouth, and often a dusky-to-black patch on the topside pectoral fin with a faint pale border — a mark winter flounder lacks entirely.
variants.where_found: A deeper, offshore species, uncommon in the shallow shore/estuary water winter flounder are typically caught from.
variants.notes: Counts toward the same groundfish aggregate limit as winter flounder — no separate rule, just useful for ID if one turns up on deeper boat gear.
